title: The Mary Celeste: Why Did 10 People Abandon a Sound Ship?
case_meta: North Atlantic, near the Azores · December 1872
subject: celeste
description:
Would you have left the ship? What do you think Captain Briggs saw that morning? 👇

In December 1872 the crew of the Dei Gratia found the Mary Celeste drifting east of the Azores with her cargo intact, food for six months and nobody aboard. This case file follows the voyage, the Gibraltar salvage hearing, the nine empty barrels and the theories, from alcohol fumes to a faulty pump.

Sources: Wikipedia, "Mary Celeste" and its references; Smithsonian Magazine; Encyclopaedia Britannica; University College London (Andrea Sella, 2006); Smithsonian Channel, "The True Story of the Mary Celeste" (2007).

scenes.text: The two ships were about four hundred miles east of the Azores when the lookout noticed that the other vessel was steering badly, swinging off course as if no one cared where she went.
Captain David Morehouse of the Dei Gratia watched her through his glass for a long time. He could see no one at the wheel and no one on deck.
His first mate, Oliver Deveau, rowed across with two men and climbed aboard. The ship was the Mary Celeste, out of New York, and she was empty.
There was food for six months. The cargo was in place. The crew's clothes and belongings were still in their quarters, and one small boat was gone.
Ten people had sailed on her a month earlier. Not one of them was ever seen again, and the ship they left behind has been argued over ever since.
She had started life as the Amazon, built in 1861 at Spencer's Island in Nova Scotia. After she ran aground in 1867, American owners rebuilt her and renamed her Mary Celeste.
Her captain in 1872 was Benjamin Spooner Briggs, thirty-seven, from Marion, Massachusetts. He came from a family of sea captains and owned a share of the ship himself.
He brought his wife, Sarah, and their two-year-old daughter, Sophia. Their seven-year-old son, Arthur, stayed at home with his grandmother so he could go to school.
Sarah also brought her melodeon, a small reed organ, and set it up in the cabin. It was still there when the ship was found.
The crew was small. The first mate was Albert Richardson, an American. Most of the seamen were Germans, among them two brothers named Lorenzen.
Below deck sat the cargo: 1,701 barrels of industrial alcohol, bound for Genoa in Italy. It was valuable, and it was flammable.
Before sailing, Briggs wrote to his mother that the vessel was in beautiful trim and that he hoped for a fine passage. Then bad weather held them off Staten Island for two days.
On the seventh of November 1872 the Mary Celeste put to sea. The Dei Gratia, carrying petroleum to Gibraltar, left New York about a week later on a similar course.
Deveau searched the ship from bow to stern. Between decks it was soaked, and there were about three and a half feet of water in the hold.
That was a lot, but not enough to sink her. Deveau later told the court that the hull was sound. One of the two pumps had been taken apart.
On deck lay a sounding rod, the simple tool used to measure how much water a ship has taken on. Someone had been checking.

scenes.text: Several things were missing: the chronometer, the sextant, the ship's register and the small yawl that served as her lifeboat. Whoever left had taken the means to navigate.
The logbook stayed behind. Its last entry was dated the twenty-fourth of November. On the slate used for daily notes, a final line from the morning of the twenty-fifth gave her position.
She was passing Santa Maria, the easternmost island of the Azores. After that, the record stops. For about nine days the ship had sailed on alone.
Morehouse split his small crew. Deveau and two sailors took the Mary Celeste to Gibraltar, where she arrived on the thirteenth of December, a day behind the Dei Gratia.
The Dei Gratia's crew claimed salvage, a share of the value of the ship they had saved. The case went before the Vice Admiralty Court in Gibraltar.
The Attorney General there, Frederick Solly-Flood, did not believe their story. He suspected the crew of the Mary Celeste had got drunk on the cargo and murdered the Briggs family.
He pointed to marks along the bow, to stains on the rail and the deck, and to a sword found in the captain's cabin.
A government surveyor, John Austin, examined the ship. He found no sign of a fight. The marks on the bow, he reported, looked like ordinary damage from the sea.
The stains were tested. The results said they were not blood, but Solly-Flood did not make that public for years.
He then turned his suspicion on Morehouse and Deveau. Had the two crews arranged the whole thing together to collect the money? No evidence of that was ever found.
In March 1873 the court awarded the Dei Gratia's owners and crew £1,700. That was far less than they had hoped for, and some historians read it as a sign of the court's lingering doubts.
The Mary Celeste finally reached Genoa with her cargo. When the barrels were unloaded, nine of the 1,701 were found to be empty.
Those nine were made of red oak, a more porous wood than the white oak of the others. Alcohol could have soaked through them, or leaked away during the voyage.
To many writers, that detail mattered. A leaking alcohol cargo meant fumes in a closed hold, on a wooden ship with a stove in the galley.
Other facts did not fit any neat story. The hatches had been opened, but the ship was not on fire, and nothing had been burned.
Nobody had tried to steal anything. The family's possessions were left behind in the cabin, along with the crew's clothes, the melodeon and most of the ship's stores.
And the yawl was gone. That was the one clear clue. Ten people had climbed into an open boat in the middle of the Atlantic and left a floating ship behind.
Then came the fiction. In 1884 a young doctor named Arthur Conan Doyle published a story in the Cornhill Magazine about a ship he called the Marie Celeste.
His tale of revenge and murder was invented, but many readers took it as fact. Its misspelled name and its invented details still appear in retellings today.
Of the real theories, piracy is the weakest. Pirates would have taken the cargo and the valuables, and nothing of value had been touched.
Mutiny has a similar problem. Austin found no sign of a struggle, and a mutinous crew would hardly trade a sound ship and its cargo for an open boat.
The most popular idea is the alcohol itself. Some believe fumes built up in the hold, and that Briggs, fearing an explosion, ordered everyone into the boat to wait at a safe distance.
In 2006, the chemist Andrea Sella of University College London tested this in a model of the hold. The vapour burned in a sudden flash that left no scorch marks behind.
Others point to the water. If Briggs had a faulty pump and a sounding that looked much worse than it was, he might have believed his ship was sinking.
A seaquake, a waterspout and a sudden squall have all been suggested too. Each could explain a moment of panic, but none of them left evidence anyone could prove.
In 2007, the researcher Anne MacGregor brought the water and the map together. Her work became the basis of a Smithsonian Channel documentary that year.
According to her research, the ship's chronometer may have been wrong, placing Briggs well off his true course. The vessel had also recently carried coal, which could have clogged the pumps.
In her view, Briggs found water rising, could not pump it out, and saw Santa Maria close by. The island was the last land before Europe. He made for it in the boat.
If the line from the yawl parted, or the wind filled the empty sails, the ship would have pulled away from them. An open boat could not catch it.
It is a careful theory, and it fits the dismantled pump and the sounding rod. But it cannot be proven. The yawl and its passengers were never found.
The Mary Celeste herself sailed on for another twelve years. In 1885 her last captain wrecked her on a reef off Haiti in an attempt at insurance fraud.
Back in Marion, Arthur Briggs grew up without his parents or his sister. His father's last letter had promised a fine passage.
Somewhere near Santa Maria, ten people stepped into a small boat and watched a sound ship sail away without anyone at the wheel, and no record says what happened to them next.
